header.name: New Media and Politics
header.description: Conventional views on the global rise of populism, fake news and extreme polarisation evaluate these in terms of the 'the failure of the neoliberal economics' and/or a result of 'destabilised cultural identity'. But could this have happened without the Internet? This course offers a 'new' media perspective to answer this puzzle, and combines varied explanations to develop macro- level theoretical insights around contemporary politics and implications for policy and regulation. (In PART I) we begin by questioning the binaries in debates around 'hacktivism' which either ignore the difference between old and new media or adopts a heavy ‘technological determinism’ in their explanations. Instead, we develop arguments around the newness of Internet-enabled political action, covering key and historical and technological development relating to spatial nature of new populism ('counter public sphere' Fraser 1992), social movements (Wellman and Raini 2012) as well as communicative power (Castells 2009). (In PART II) we consider several prominent case studies and examples to evaluate these theoretical and conceptual insights. We begin with the 'occupy' movements that spread across the world after the financial crisis in early 2010s, and then analyse the use of new media in the uprisings in Arab world and Asia. Taking a series of case studies we theorise the power of Twitter, Facebook and WhatsApp as 'new' intermediaries and analyse the populist trend in terms of the changing balance between the state and society and the slow erosion of established institutions. These cases focus primarily on populist politics but also include new environmental movements, civic activism and digital journalism. In terms of pedagogical approach, and evaluating criteria, our course will rely on active learning that requires all students to develop a strong research orientation and would help them devlop independent projects that showcase these insights in terms of policy analysis, journalism as well as technology development.

outcomes.label: CO1
outcomes.raw_text: Students will begin by recalling and critically questioning conventional assumptions and technological deterministic claims about online media and their effects

outcomes.label: CO2
outcomes.raw_text: Having done away with conventional views, students will learn to classify and discuss key concepts in 'new' political processes, develop a political map of internet since the Cold-War era, in the process lelearning key communicative, spatial and social dimensions of these technological developments

outcomes.label: CO3
outcomes.raw_text: Moving on, students will then learn to independently apply and critique theories of networked individualism in relation to the emergence of (un)mediated public sphere and correlate it with the rise of populism in the 21st century

outcomes.label: CO4
outcomes.raw_text: Students will independently undertake research projects to hypothesize role of new media and its relation to populist politics, with a focus on South Asia and India

outcomes.label: CO5
outcomes.raw_text: Students will be able to respond to, and develop new policy guidelines for the future and construct alternative perspectives from to the thinking of the state on the question of new media and the internet.
